Title: Simulating soil fertility and poverty dynamics in Uganda: A bio-economic multi-agent systems approach
Authors: Pepijn Schreinemachers; Thomas Berger; Jens B. Aune
Geographical_Context: Magada and Buyemba villages, Lake Victoria Crescent, south-eastern Uganda
Agricultural_Domain: Crop and farm management; Soil fertility/nutrient management; Technology adoption; Rural poverty and livelihoods
Study_Objective: Demonstrate a bio-economic multi-agent modelling approach that integrates heterogeneous farm-household decisions with soil-fertility dynamics, and assess how short-term credit, mineral fertiliser and improved maize seed affect poverty and ecological sustainability.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate heterogeneous farm-household investment, production, consumption and technology-adoption decisions together with soil-nutrient/crop-yield dynamics for ex-ante agricultural policy assessment.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Integrated bio-economic model; Policy-analysis/decision-support framework
Agent_Roles: Each farm-household agent makes investment, production and consumption decisions, manages crops/livestock and household resources, and may adopt innovations according to peer-network diffusion rules.
Decision_Mechanism: Recursive mathematical programming for household utility/economic optimisation; threshold-based peer technology diffusion; coupled Tropical Soil Productivity Calculator for soil/crop dynamics
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each household independently solves agent-specific investment, production and consumption problems under its own land, labour, capital, demographic and soil constraints; innovation adoption is influenced by the share of peer agents that already adopted.
Input_Information: Household resources and demographics; land/plot location; soil fertility; crop/livestock options; prices; labour; credit access; crop yields; fertiliser and improved-seed availability; peer adoption; soil N/P/K/organic carbon/pH
MAS_Platform_Technology: MP-MAS implemented in object-oriented C++; recursive mathematical programming; Tropical Soil Productivity Calculator (TSPC); Excel/ASCII model inputs
Coordination_Mechanism: Peer-network technology diffusion; no central agricultural coordinator is used in this Uganda application.
Communication_Mechanism: Peer/social-network observation of innovation adoption; no formal message protocol is reported.
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Land; Labour; Household capital/credit; Fertiliser and improved seed; Crop/livestock production; Soil nutrients
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Maximise household economic/food-consumption objectives under resource constraints while assessing poverty and soil-fertility consequences of credit and technology policies.
Conflict_Resolution: NA — this application does not model an explicit shared-resource conflict-resolution mechanism.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: No explicit inter-household competition for a shared resource is modelled; each household balances competing internal demands for land, labour, capital, food and investment.
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Section 4.2 agent decision model; technology-diffusion component in Section 4; discussion of agent interaction
Agricultural_Outcomes: Credit and improved technologies increase household food consumption/well-being and crop productivity but do not eliminate poverty.
Livestock_Outcomes: Livestock activities are represented within household farm plans, but no livestock-specific outcome is reported as a focal result.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Improved access to credit/fertiliser/seed relaxes household capital and input constraints and increases plant-available nitrogen and production.
Environmental_Outcomes: Mineral fertiliser increases plant-available nitrogen, but simulated total soil nitrogen stocks do not improve, so long-term ecological sustainability is not ensured.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Improved input/technology access is evaluated, but the analysed package does not include a sufficient soil-conservation mechanism to maintain long-term soil-N stocks.
Quantitative_Results: Baseline poverty incidence was 28.9%; credit reduced it to 24.4% (15.3% reduction), while credit plus improved technologies reduced it to 19.8%, with 31.3% of agents moving across the poverty line relative to baseline. Fertiliser increased plant-available N but did not improve total soil-N stocks.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Short-term poverty/productivity gains from credit, fertiliser and improved seed versus limited improvement in long-term soil-fertility/ecological sustainability.
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Empirical calibration; Model validation; Comparative scenario evaluation
Evaluation_Environment: 15-year MP-MAS simulation of 520 heterogeneous farm-household agents coupled to soil-fertility/crop-yield dynamics in two Ugandan villages.
Data_Source: Uganda National Household Survey; IFPRI farm-household survey; ZEF-Bonn village survey; geo-referenced soil samples; digital elevation model; literature/secondary biophysical data
Experimental_Scenarios: Baseline continuation; short-term credit for mineral fertiliser and improved maize seed; credit plus unrestricted access to the selected innovations.
Baselines_Comparators: Baseline scenario continuing current dynamics; observed survey/field indicators used for validation.
Evaluation_Metrics: Poverty/food-energy consumption; land-use shares; crop yields; intercropping; nutrient balances; soil N/available N; observed-vs-simulated fit; household well-being
Evaluation_Results: The model reproduces key land-use, yield, intercropping and consumption patterns with quantitative validation; policy scenarios indicate substantial poverty reduction but weak long-term soil-N improvement.
Evaluation_Scale: 520 farm-household agents; two villages covering about 12 km²; 15-year simulation horizon
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Environmental modelling; Other — omitted shocks
Reported_Limitations: Historical data for dynamic validation were unavailable, so evaluation relied on one-step validation and literature benchmarks. The model omits pests and stochastic weather/price shocks that could reduce simulated technology benefits.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Compare alternative price conditions; incorporate soil-conservation measures and additional uncertainty; strengthen longitudinal/dynamic validation when historical data become available.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Section 5 Model validation; Sections 6–7; conclusion/discussion of validation challenges
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (B17). Pre-2010 foundational study retained under IC7. Uses the MP-MAS research platform also represented elsewhere in the corpus; study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: An adaptive multi-agent model for water allocation under scarcity: application of bankruptcy methods
Geographical_Context: Zarrinehrud River Basin, Lake Urmia Basin, Iran; Bukan Dam and 11 agricultural sub-basins
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Reservoir operation; Agricultural water allocation; Water-governance fairness
Study_Objective: Develop an adaptive multi-agent framework for fair and economically efficient reservoir-water allocation across severe-drought, dry, normal and wet conditions while incorporating farmer behavioural heterogeneity and reducing conflict.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Allocate scarce reservoir water among heterogeneous agricultural agents adaptively, balancing total net profit, fairness and financial satisfaction under changing hydrological conditions.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Water-allocation/coordination mechanism; Decision-support/optimisation framework
Agent_Roles: Eleven agricultural agents represent grouped farmers, each with water demand, utility/net-profit function and selfishness coefficient; the reservoir-operation layer forecasts supply, determines monthly releases and allocates available agricultural water.
Decision_Mechanism: Genetic-algorithm adaptive reservoir operation; penalty-based decentralised optimisation in dry/normal/wet conditions; bankruptcy/cooperative-game allocation (PRO, CEA, CEL, PIN, FPS, PPS, PIS) in severe drought; Theory-of-Planned-Behavior-derived selfishness coefficients
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Each agricultural agent maximises its own net-profit utility subject to water and behavioural constraints; allocation is coordinated by reservoir-operation rules, while severe scarcity invokes bankruptcy rules that redistribute water/profit among agents.
Input_Information: Reservoir storage; forecast inflow/precipitation; agricultural/domestic/industrial/environmental demands; agent water claims; crop productivity/net profit; selfishness coefficients; education, income, machinery access, spatial position and other TPB behavioural criteria
MAS_Platform_Technology: SWAT; numerical weather prediction ensemble and bias correction; long-term reservoir optimisation; genetic algorithm; multi-agent utility model; bankruptcy methods; Jain fairness index
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Section 2 methodology and multi-agent model; Section 3 Study Area; Figure 1
Coordination_Mechanism: Adaptive reservoir release plus decentralised penalty allocation; bankruptcy/cooperative-game rules and profit redistribution under severe scarcity
Communication_Mechanism: Shared coordinator/reservoir-allocation state and rule-based allocation; behavioural influence is parameterised through social/psychological factors rather than a formal message protocol.
Information_Shared: Available reservoir water; agent demands/claims; productivity; net-profit values; allocation/satisfaction levels; behavioural/selfishness information
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Reservoir water allocated to agriculture and among 11 agricultural agents
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Maximise agricultural net profit while improving fairness and financial satisfaction and reducing conflict under water scarcity.
Conflict_Resolution: Penalty functions manage ordinary shortages; severe drought triggers bankruptcy rules. Proposed FPS/PPS/PIS schemes reprioritise water and/or redistribute profit to mitigate inequity and dissatisfaction.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Eleven agricultural agents compete for limited reservoir water; agricultural demand also coexists with domestic, industrial and environmental demands.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Monthly agricultural demands; reservoir storage/inflow; hydrological condition; productivity and utility functions; selfishness coefficients; supply-to-demand ratio; behavioural and spatial criteria
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Section 2 adaptive reservoir operation and bankruptcy methods; Section 3; Tables 1–3; Figures 1 and 3
Agricultural_Outcomes: Water allocation changes farm-agent financial returns and satisfaction under severe drought, favouring different productivity/vulnerability profiles depending on the rule used.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Adaptive allocation directs scarce water toward higher-value uses while proposed rules explicitly trade economic efficiency against distributional fairness.
Environmental_Outcomes: The framework manages agricultural withdrawals under hydrological scarcity and includes environmental water demand, but long-term ecological outcomes are not directly quantified.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Adaptive reservoir operation, scarcity-aware allocation, environmental-demand constraints and proposed future incentives for sustainable irrigation practices
Quantitative_Results: During severe drought, Jain fairness/net profit (million USD) were PRO 0.97/4.76, CEA 0.85/6.35, CEL 0.31/2.17, PIN 0.84/6.31, FPS 0.72/6.55, PPS 0.72/6.53 and PIS 0.49/2.14. FPS generated +0.20, +4.38, +1.79 and +0.24 million USD relative to CEA, CEL, PRO and PIN, respectively.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Fairness versus economic efficiency/profit; highly productive-agent prioritisation versus protection/compensation of vulnerable agents.
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Section 4 Results and Discussion; Figure 6; Table 5; Section 5 Conclusions
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Comparative method evaluation; Sensitivity/forecast validation
Evaluation_Environment: Adaptive reservoir-operation simulation for Bukan Dam/Zarrinehrud Basin using NWP precipitation forecasts, SWAT inflows and 11 agricultural agents.
Data_Source: Hydrometeorological and reservoir data; NWP forecasts; SWAT inputs; National Cartographic Center shapefiles; water-demand records; reports and questionnaires used for agent behavioural criteria
Experimental_Scenarios: Severe drought, dry, normal and wet conditions; seven bankruptcy allocation rules under severe drought; adaptive monthly operation over an eight-month planning period.
Baselines_Comparators: Classical bankruptcy rules PRO, CEA, CEL and PIN compared with proposed FPS, PPS and PIS; penalty-based allocation used outside severe drought.
Evaluation_Metrics: Total agricultural net profit; Jain fairness index; supply-to-demand/satisfaction ratios; agent financial satisfaction; reservoir/allocation performance
Evaluation_Results: FPS and PPS achieved the highest total profits, while PRO achieved the highest fairness; proposed profit-redistribution approaches improved vulnerable-agent financial satisfaction but did not maximise Jain fairness.
Evaluation_Scale: 11 agricultural agents/sub-basins; Zarrinehrud basin >12,000 km²; eight-month severe-drought planning evaluation
Limitation_Categories: Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Other — behavioural simplification; Other — missing social dynamics/conflict
Reported_Limitations: Selfishness coefficients and utility functions simplify complex behaviour; explicit social dynamics and inter-agent conflicts are not modelled; selfishness is static although real behaviour can learn and adapt under repeated scarcity.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Test alternative profit-redistribution criteria; study long-term sustainability and behavioural effects; improve psychological/behavioural estimation; add reinforcement-learning adaptation, water-quality dimensions, and negotiation/bargaining or coalition formation.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Section 4; Section 5 Conclusions and Future Directions; Data Availability Statement
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (F01). All relevant data are reported as included in the paper or Supplementary Information. Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: Optimal Irrigation Allocation for Large-Scale Arable Farming
Authors: A.T.J.R. Cobbenhagen; L.P.A. Schoonen; M.J.G. van de Molengraft; W.P.M.H. Heemels
Venue: IEEE Transactions on Control Systems Technology
Geographical_Context: Large-scale arable-farming simulation using historical weather from Eelde, the Netherlands
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Precision agriculture; Farm machinery/resource allocation; Crop production
Study_Objective: Develop a scalable online model-predictive-control framework that jointly allocates irrigation water and a limited fleet of irrigation machines across many fields while maximising season-level agricultural value under operational constraints.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Coordinate scarce irrigation machinery and water across heterogeneous fields to improve crop production/resource efficiency while satisfying machine capacity, travel and replenishment constraints.
Agent_Types: Irrigation-machinery/resource-delivery agents; Field/client entities; Resource store/refill locations
Agent_Roles: Irrigation-machine agents deliver water and are allocated to fields; field clients receive irrigation and evolve through crop/water dynamics; a central MPC optimiser computes daily allocations and irrigation amounts.
Decision_Mechanism: Receding-horizon model predictive control with mixed-integer optimisation, crop-growth predictions and explicit allocation/travel/refilling constraints
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Irrigation machines are modelled as resource-delivery agents but their actions are centrally scheduled by the MPC optimiser rather than selected by autonomous local policies.
Input_Information: Field crop/water states; weather forecasts; LINTUL2 crop-growth predictions; irrigation demand; machine capacities/application rates; machine-field allocation feasibility; travel distances/costs; resource-store/refilling constraints
MAS_Platform_Technology: LINTUL2 crop model; MPC; mixed-integer optimisation; historical Eelde weather data
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Sections I–V, especially problem formulation, MPC framework and case-study setup
Coordination_Mechanism: Central MPC jointly schedules irrigation amounts and machine-to-field assignments under finite fleet/resource constraints.
Communication_Mechanism: Shared-state/central-controller coordination; no explicit peer-to-peer communication protocol is reported.
Information_Shared: Field/crop/water states; predicted weather; agent availability/capacity; travel/refill state; planned irrigation amounts and assignments
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Irrigation water; Irrigation machinery; Machine travel/refilling; Daily field irrigation tasks
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Maximise long-term agricultural objective/profit proxy while using water and machinery efficiently and maintaining feasible daily allocations.
Conflict_Resolution: The central mixed-integer MPC optimiser resolves simultaneous field demand by selecting a feasible global allocation subject to machine capacity, exclusivity, travel and refill constraints.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Up to 100 fields compete for five irrigation agents and limited daily machine/resource capacity.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Soil/field water state; critical water levels; crop growth/yield prediction; weather forecast; field size; machine delivery rate/capacity; field-machine distances; refill/store constraints; irrigation cost
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Problem formulation and MPC constraints in Sections II–V; Section VI case study
Agricultural_Outcomes: The MPC increased simulated crop yield relative to the heuristic and improved the farm-level objective across most historical seasons.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Lower water use, higher water-use efficiency and higher irrigation-moment efficiency while satisfying realistic machinery-allocation constraints.
Environmental_Outcomes: Reduced irrigation-water use for higher simulated crop output.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Predictive irrigation scheduling that targets water only where/when beneficial while coordinating finite machinery.
Quantitative_Results: Across 33 seasons, MPC improved the objective by 5.31% on average (maximum 18.3%), produced 5.29% more yield and used 5.17% less water than the heuristic. Water-use efficiency was 11.64% higher and irrigation-moment efficiency 11.7% higher; daily computation averaged 3 min and peaked at 20 min.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Benefits depend on weather (small in very wet seasons, larger in dry seasons); richer travel/refilling constraints improve realism but increase optimisation/computation complexity.
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Section VI-B Results; Figures 2–3; Table I; Section VII
Evaluation_Environment: LINTUL2-based large-scale arable-farm simulation using 33 historical growing seasons and MPC solved daily.
Data_Source: LINTUL2 crop model and associated historical Eelde weather data (1966–1998/1999); model parameters from literature and agricultural practice
Experimental_Scenarios: Primary case: 100 fields, five irrigation agents and one store; 33 historical seasons with parameter/weather uncertainty. Additional travel-cost experiment: 25 fields, two agents and one store over five seasons.
Evaluation_Metrics: Objective function; final yield/WSO; irrigation water; water-use efficiency; irrigation-moment efficiency; number of allocations; computation time; travel cost
Evaluation_Results: The MPC outperformed the heuristic on average while remaining computationally feasible for daily optimisation; improvements were strongest in dry seasons and marginal in very wet seasons.
Evaluation_Scale: 100 fields and five agents in the main case; 25 fields/two agents for travel-cost study; 33 historical growing seasons
Limitation_Categories: Computational requirements; Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Other — full-state assumption
Reported_Limitations: The framework assumes full crop-state information and relies on crop/weather/model parameters; robustness to parameter uncertainty needs further analysis. Historical-practice validation and sensing/state-estimation are not yet demonstrated.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Perform broader sensitivity analysis; compare MPC recommendations with historical farm practices; develop sensing/state-estimation agents and test the framework operationally under real farm conditions.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Section VI; Section VII Conclusion and Future Work
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (F02). The authors describe this journal article as a significant extension of preliminary irrigation-MPC work represented by S53; exact study-family assignment is deferred to Step 5.

Title: Multi-Robot Task Allocation in Agriculture Scenarios Based on the Improved NSGA-II Algorithm
Authors: Zaiwang Lu; Zixu Zhao; Long Long; Yike Ma; Lei Li; Zichen Liu; Feng Dai; Yucheng Zhang; Jintao Li
Geographical_Context: Agricultural multi-robot task-allocation experiments including real task-plot data from Dahewan Farm, Inner Mongolia, China, plus TSPLIB benchmarks
Agricultural_Domain: Agricultural robotics; Task allocation; Farm machinery scheduling
Study_Objective: Formulate agricultural multi-robot task allocation as a bi-objective multiple-traveling-salesman problem and develop an improved NSGA-II algorithm that reduces total robot travel while balancing workload.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Coordinate multiple agricultural robots across spatially distributed field tasks to obtain efficient, balanced task assignments and support unmanned-farm scheduling.
Agent_Types: Agricultural robot agents; Agricultural task-plot entities; Central scheduling/monitoring layer
Agent_Roles: Robot agents execute assigned field tasks; the central framework monitors robot/task status and runs INSGA-II to generate or adjust task-allocation plans.
Decision_Mechanism: Improved NSGA-II multi-objective evolutionary optimisation with workload-balancing objective, improved initial population and adaptive genetic operators
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Robots are treated as execution agents whose task sets/routes are assigned centrally; the scheduling framework can be re-triggered as robot or task status changes.
Input_Information: Task-plot coordinates; plot workload; number/status of robots; travel distances; existing task-allocation state
MAS_Platform_Technology: INSGA-II implemented/evaluated in MATLAB; TSPLIB benchmark instances; agricultural task-plot dataset
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Sections II–IV; system/task-allocation formulation; algorithm description
Coordination_Mechanism: Central multi-objective optimisation allocates task plots/routes among robots while minimising total distance and balancing workload.
Communication_Mechanism: Central monitoring of robot/task status and dissemination of updated allocation plans; no explicit robot-to-robot protocol is described.
Information_Shared: Robot status; task status; plot coordinates; workload; assigned routes/tasks
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Agricultural field tasks; Robot workload; Robot travel/routes
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Minimise total robot travel distance while balancing workload across the available robot fleet.
Conflict_Resolution: The optimiser enforces one assignment per task and searches Pareto-efficient solutions for the distance/workload objectives.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Multiple robots share the finite set of agricultural task plots, with competing objectives of short travel and balanced workload.
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Problem formulation and framework in Sections II–III; experimental setup in Section IV
Agricultural_Outcomes: More efficient multi-robot field-task plans are generated for unmanned/agricultural operations; no crop-yield outcome is evaluated.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Substantially shorter total robot travel in most benchmark/real-farm cases, with explicit workload balancing.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Indirect efficiency benefit through reduced robot travel; energy/emissions are not evaluated.
Quantitative_Results: For the real farmdata40 case with three robots, INSGA-II reduced total travel distance from 30,975.2891 (NSGA-II) and 26,310.7176 (GA) to 19,262.4700, while its workload-imbalance objective was 8,613 versus 2,330 for NSGA-II. Across TSPLIB and farmdata40, experiments were repeated 20 times and INSGA-II generally produced the shortest total distance.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Travel-distance minimisation versus workload balance; the improved algorithm can achieve much shorter distance at the cost of a less favourable workload-balance objective in some cases.
RQ3_Evidence_Locator: Section IV Experimental Results; Tables I–II; Figure 5
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Comparative algorithm evaluation; Benchmark evaluation
Evaluation_Environment: MATLAB experiments on four TSPLIB benchmark datasets and one real agricultural task-plot dataset from Dahewan Farm.
Data_Source: Public TSPLIB benchmark instances; real agricultural task-plot coordinates/workload from Dahewan Farm, Inner Mongolia
Experimental_Scenarios: Robot fleet sizes of 1, 3 and 5 across berlin52, pr76, kroA100, eil101 and farmdata40; population size 100, 1000 iterations and 20 repeated runs.
Baselines_Comparators: Standard NSGA-II; Genetic Algorithm (GA); TSPLIB known solutions for single-robot comparisons
Evaluation_Metrics: Total travel distance; workload-balance objective; Pareto-front quality/distribution; benchmark best distance
Evaluation_Results: INSGA-II generally produced denser/better Pareto fronts and lower total travel distance than NSGA-II and GA across the tested datasets and robot counts.
Evaluation_Scale: 40–101 task locations; 1, 3 or 5 robots; five datasets; 20 repeated runs per parameter setting
Limitation_Categories: Real-world validation; Other — simplified travel metric; Other — collision/path-planning omission
Reported_Limitations: Travel between task plots is represented by Euclidean distance rather than executable field routes, and collision-free multi-robot transfer/path planning is not included.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Improve algorithm performance; test additional methods and more realistic scenarios; integrate true field-route planning, collision-free transfers and a complete unmanned-farm scheduling system.
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (F03). Public TSPLIB benchmarks are accessible; availability of the Dahewan farm dataset itself is not clearly reported. Study-family reconciliation deferred to Step 5.

Title: Fostering local crop-livestock integration via legume exchanges using an innovative integrated assessment and modelling approach based on the MAELIA platform
Authors: Rui Catarino; Olivier Therond; Jérémy Berthomier; Maurice Miara; Emmanuel Mérot; Renaud Misslin; Paul Vanhove; Jean Villerd; Frédérique Angevin
Geographical_Context: Pays de Pouzauges, Vendée, western France; collective of five arable and two dairy-livestock farms
Agricultural_Domain: Crop-livestock integration; Crop/farm planning; Feed self-sufficiency; Agroecological sustainability
Study_Objective: Use MAELIA and participatory scenario design to assess self-sufficiency, sustainability and vulnerability at farm, farm-group and territorial levels as cooperation and legume/feed exchanges between specialised arable and livestock farms increase.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Simulate coordinated crop-livestock territorial integration and local feed exchanges, evaluating how alternative cooperation/rotation strategies affect collective self-sufficiency and multi-dimensional sustainability.
Contribution_Type: Simulation model; Integrated assessment; Decision-support framework; Participatory scenario analysis
Agent_Types: Arable-farmer agents; Livestock-farmer agents; Field/crop entities
Agent_Roles: Arable farmers implement crop rotations and management and supply feed crops; livestock farmers demand feed ingredients for dairy rations; farm agents participate in progressively more coordinated local exchange scenarios.
Decision_Mechanism: MAELIA daily IF-THEN farm/technical-operation rules coupled to AqYield crop dynamics; participatory scenario rules for coexistence, complementarity and synergetic crop/feed coordination
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Farm agents execute farm-specific technical rules using local field, weather and workload states; inter-farm exchange/coordination intensity is imposed by the co-designed scenario rather than emerging through endogenous negotiation.
Input_Information: Farm/field boundaries; crop rotations; soil and climate; crop-management rules; farm prices/costs; feed formulation and livestock feed demand; labour/workload; yields; input use
MAS_Platform_Technology: MAELIA spatial agent-based platform; AqYield crop model; French LPIS/GIS; SAFRAN climate data; participatory scenario design
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Sections 2.2–2.5; scenario design and MAELIA description
Coordination_Mechanism: Local farm-to-farm feed exchange and progressively stronger coordination: coexistence market exchange, complementarity through introduced legumes, and synergetic collaborative crop-rotation planning.
Communication_Mechanism: Scenario-defined bilateral/multilateral exchange and collaborative planning; no formal dynamic agent-message protocol is reported.
Information_Shared: Feed supply/demand; crop/rotation plans; farm production; prices/costs; required legume and maize-silage quantities
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Feed crops/protein; Agricultural land and crop rotations; Nitrogen fertiliser; Farm labour; Local crop-livestock material flows
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Meet local livestock feed/protein demand while maintaining viable farm economics and improving territorial environmental/social performance.
Conflict_Resolution: Coordination is resolved ex ante through participatory scenario design and collaborative crop-rotation/feed-exchange rules; no endogenous bargaining mechanism is simulated.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Individual farm profitability/land-use preferences can conflict with collective feed self-sufficiency, coordinated rotations and territorial environmental goals.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Weather/soil/crop state and farm rules are represented in MAELIA; irrigation is not the focal coordination decision in this study.
RQ2_Evidence_Locator: Section 2.4 scenario design; Section 3 self-sufficiency results; Section 4.2 organisational barriers
Agricultural_Outcomes: The synergetic scenario achieved territorial legume/feed self-sufficiency and improved average territorial gross margin, though gains/losses were heterogeneous among individual farms.
Livestock_Outcomes: Local crop exchanges supplied the reformulated dairy feed; new formulations reduced annual feed cost by 16% for LF1 and 7% for LF2 while milk production/quality were held constant by design.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Reduced nitrogen-fertiliser use and labour requirement; local protein/feed substitution reduces dependence on imported soybean meal and external inputs.
Environmental_Outcomes: Territorial nitrogen-fertiliser use decreased, while pesticide active-ingredient use rose slightly on average and increased substantially on some farms; broader GHG/N-cycle outcomes were not modelled.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Legume-based crop diversification; local protein/feed exchanges; longer rotations; reduced mineral-N dependence
Quantitative_Results: Synergetic coordination achieved local feed self-sufficiency; territorial mean gross margin increased by 71 €/ha (4%), nitrogen-fertiliser use decreased by about 21 kg N/ha (11%), and labour time decreased by about 12 min/ha (5%). New livestock feed formulations reduced feed costs by 16% and 7% per cow/year for LF1 and LF2. Pesticide use increased slightly overall and by up to 37% for one arable farm.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Collective self-sufficiency/sustainability versus unequal individual farm gains; lower N use and labour versus possible pesticide increases; territorial benefits versus transaction/coordination costs.
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Participatory validation; Comparative scenario evaluation
Evaluation_Environment: MAELIA simulation of seven real farms over August 2004–December 2017 with participatory calibration/validation and farm-to-territory indicators.
Data_Source: Farmers and agricultural advisers; French LPIS field data; SAFRAN climate; European soil data plus farmer soil analyses; agricultural prices/costs; farm rotations and management; supplementary study data
Experimental_Scenarios: Baseline; coexistence; complementarity; synergetic territorial crop-livestock integration
Baselines_Comparators: Baseline specialised farms with no inter-farm feed trade
Evaluation_Metrics: Feed and protein self-sufficiency; energy/protein yield; gross margin; economic efficiency; N-fertiliser use; pesticide active ingredients; workload; temporal trend and variability/vulnerability
Evaluation_Results: Only the strongest synergetic coordination consistently met local legume/feed needs; it improved several territorial economic/environmental/social indicators and reduced vulnerability, but benefits varied markedly among farms.
Evaluation_Scale: Five arable and two livestock farms; 13-year simulation; indicators at farm, farm-group and territory levels
Limitation_Categories: Environmental modelling; Real-world validation; Uncertainty; Adoption/usability; Other — context dependence; Other — data/calibration burden
Reported_Limitations: Livestock/grassland dynamics, animal-waste production, soil N cycling/emissions, pest damage and pesticide effects are omitted; only seven farms in a small territory are studied, making findings context-dependent. Data collection/formatting/calibration is time-consuming.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Add livestock and nutrient/emissions dynamics and broader environmental indicators; test climate/economic sensitivity; replicate in other social contexts and larger territories; study contracts, transaction costs and farmer collaboration.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Section 2.5; Section 4 Discussion; Section 5 Conclusion; Appendix A Supplementary Data
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (F04). Uses the MAELIA research platform already represented in the corpus; related-publication/study-family assignment is deferred to Step 5.

Title: Multi-actor approach to manage the water-energy-food nexus at territory scale
Authors: Amaya Saint-Bois; Marianne Boix; Olivier Therond; Ludovic Montastruc; Jean Villerd; Iréa Touche
Geographical_Context: Downstream Aveyron watershed, south-western France; approximately 800 km² and 15,024 agricultural parcels
Agricultural_Domain: Water-energy-food nexus; Agricultural land allocation; Irrigation/water management; Renewable energy integration
Study_Objective: Develop a generic multi-level multi-actor framework that combines operational multi-agent water-food simulations with strategic multi-criteria decision making to allocate agricultural and renewable-energy land uses under water constraints.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Support local/regional land-use and water-energy-food decisions by simulating farm-water dynamics and evaluating crop, agrivoltaic, photovoltaic and wind alternatives across an agricultural territory.
Contribution_Type: Platform/framework; Simulation model; Decision-support system; Multi-criteria land-allocation method
Agent_Types: Farmer agents; Water-management/dam agents; State/regulatory actors; Agricultural parcel/field entities
Agent_Roles: Farmer agents perform crop/irrigation operations; water-management actors regulate withdrawals and dam releases; parcel entities carry spatial land-use alternatives; strategic local/regional methods select land allocations from operational simulation outputs.
Decision_Mechanism: MAELIA operational/tactical agent rules; crop/hydrology simulation; Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP); Monte Carlo/Pareto regional search; multi-criteria aggregation
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Operational farm/water actors act under local biophysical and regulatory rules, while higher-level strategic decision methods use aggregated simulation indicators to choose parcel- or territory-level land allocations.
Input_Information: Parcel/land-use data; crop/irrigation management; soil and weather; river flow and dam release; agricultural gross margins/workload; renewable-energy suitability/yield; photovoltaic/wind economics and footprint; multi-criteria weights
MAS_Platform_Technology: MAELIA on GAMA; SWAT-derived hydrology; crop models including AqYield; GIS/QGIS; AHP; Monte Carlo/Pareto analysis; Python post-processing
Coordination_Mechanism: Hierarchical operational/tactical farm-water coordination in MAELIA plus strategic local/regional multi-criteria land-allocation decisions.
Communication_Mechanism: Primarily shared-state/environment-mediated coordination through water/parcel states and information flow from MAELIA outputs to strategic AHP/Monte Carlo decision layers.
Information_Shared: Crop/parcel state; river flow; irrigation withdrawals; dam releases; gross margins/workload; water, food and energy performance indicators; land-use alternative scores
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Agricultural land; Irrigation water; Food/crop production; Solar/wind energy siting; Dam/river water
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Identify land-use allocations that perform well across water, food, energy, economic, environmental-footprint and social/workload criteria under water scarcity.
Conflict_Resolution: Multi-criteria AHP and Pareto/Monte Carlo methods reconcile competing sectoral indicators at local/regional decision levels; operational water conflicts are handled by MAELIA regulation and shared hydrological constraints.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Crop production competes with renewable-energy land use; agricultural water demand competes with water-availability/river-flow constraints; local versus regional criteria can favour different allocations.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Crop/soil/water state; meteorology; irrigation strategy; river flow; dam/storage/release; water regulation; parcel land-use alternative
Agricultural_Outcomes: Under the selected indicator set, strategic methods favour 100% photovoltaic allocation over agricultural alternatives, which the authors explicitly identify as socially/food-system unrealistic without additional policy/indicator representation.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: The framework identifies parcel/territorial combinations of water, crop land and renewable-energy uses and quantifies computational/resource trade-offs; photovoltaic scenarios reduce agricultural water pressure but displace food production.
Environmental_Outcomes: Water availability/low-flow impacts and renewable-energy ecological footprints are evaluated; full dynamic energy-water feedback is incomplete in the current MAELIA implementation.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Strategic siting of PV/agrivoltaic/wind alternatives combined with water-aware agricultural simulation and multi-criteria selection
Quantitative_Results: The case study covers ~800 km² and 15,024 parcels (16,061 parcel entities after spatial subdivision). A 10-year 100%-agriculture MAELIA simulation took 31 h 22 min; indicator processing took <50 min; local and first regional methods required ~33 h total, while the second regional method required ~38 h. All three strategic methods selected a 100% PV-type solution under the chosen criteria, which the authors judged non-viable for the agricultural territory.
Tradeoffs_Reported: Food production/farmer employment versus renewable-energy value and water benefits; local versus regional decision criteria; model realism versus computational tractability; omitted subsidies/social criteria can reverse preferred land allocations.
Evaluation_Type: Simulation; Case study; Comparative decision-method evaluation; Computational-performance evaluation
Evaluation_Environment: Ten-year MAELIA/GIS simulation of an 800-km² agricultural watershed coupled to renewable-energy models and three local/regional decision methods.
Data_Source: French LPIS/GIS; meteorology; soil and crop-management data; MAELIA hydrology/water data; agricultural economic data; renewable-energy technical/economic/LCA parameters; supplementary material
Experimental_Scenarios: Uniform 100% agriculture, agrivoltaic, 100% photovoltaic and wind alternatives; local AHP and two regional decision methods using simulated parcel/territory indicators.
Baselines_Comparators: 100% agricultural reference scenario; uniform land-use alternatives; comparison of local AHP and two regional methods
Evaluation_Metrics: Agricultural and PV energy; crop protein; PV net present value; agricultural gross margin; ecological footprints; water indicator/low-water-rate frequency; farmer workload; computation time
Evaluation_Results: All strategic methods favoured 100% PV under the implemented indicator set, exposing sensitivity to omitted agricultural subsidies and incomplete social/food criteria. The first regional approximation can produce incoherent indicator predictions, and the authors recommend using it for ranking known scenarios rather than exact prediction.
Evaluation_Scale: 800 km²; 15,024 parcels/16,061 parcel entities; ten-year simulation; local parcel and regional territory decision levels
Limitation_Categories: Environmental modelling; Computational requirements; Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Adoption/usability; Reproducibility/data availability
Reported_Limitations: MAELIA simulates water-food but not complete dynamic energy interactions; PV/wind effects on hydrology/yield are approximated rather than operationally simulated. Agricultural subsidies are omitted, the social indicator overlooks energy-sector jobs, one regional approximation can be inaccurate, and data are only available on request.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Extend MAELIA to full operational WEF dynamics; model energy installations' effects on water and yields; incorporate agricultural subsidies and broader social indicators; improve regional optimisation/approximation and stakeholder-grounded decision support.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Section 4.4 Computational performances; Section 5 Discussion; Data Availability statement
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (F05). MAELIA-based multi-level extension; family relationship to existing MAELIA publications will be decided in Step 5.

Title: Optimal irrigation management for large-scale arable farming using model predictive control
Authors: L.P.A. Schoonen; A.T.J.R. Cobbenhagen; W.P.M.H. Heemels
Geographical_Context: Large-scale arable-farming simulation using historical weather from Eelde, the Netherlands
Agricultural_Domain: Irrigation/water management; Precision agriculture; Farm machinery/resource allocation
Study_Objective: Develop a model-predictive-control framework that jointly determines irrigation amounts and allocation of a limited number of irrigation machines across many arable fields to maximise end-of-season profit.
MAS_Application_Purpose: Coordinate limited irrigation machinery and water across many fields while linking short-term irrigation actions to long-term crop yield/profit.
Agent_Roles: Irrigation agents deliver water to selected fields; fields are clients whose crop/water states evolve; a central MPC computes daily irrigation quantities and agent-field assignments.
Decision_Mechanism: Receding-horizon model predictive control and mixed-integer optimisation using LINTUL2 crop/water dynamics
Agent_Autonomy_Description: Irrigation machines are represented as agents but their allocation/actions are selected centrally by the MPC optimisation framework.
Input_Information: Field soil-water/crop states; historical/forecast weather; LINTUL2 growth response; irrigation amount/cost; machine availability/capacity; crop price; critical soil-water thresholds
MAS_Platform_Technology: LINTUL2; MPC; SCIP optimisation; MATLAB simulations
RQ1_Evidence_Locator: Sections 1–3; multi-agent resource-allocation formulation and MPC framework
Coordination_Mechanism: Central MPC jointly allocates limited irrigation agents and irrigation amounts across fields.
Communication_Mechanism: Shared-state/central-controller coordination; no explicit peer-to-peer message protocol is modelled.
Information_Shared: Field/crop/water state; weather prediction; agent availability; planned irrigation amounts/assignments
Managed_Resource_or_Task: Irrigation water; Irrigation machinery; Daily field irrigation tasks
Allocation_or_Coordination_Objective: Maximise season-end profit while respecting limited machine capacity and reducing unnecessary irrigation.
Conflict_Resolution: The central optimiser resolves competing field demands by selecting a feasible agent-to-field allocation and irrigation schedule under machine/resource constraints.
Competing_Agents_or_Demands: Thirty fields compete for three irrigation agents in the main multi-field experiment.
Irrigation_Decision_Inputs: Soil water; critical/field-capacity thresholds; crop growth/yield prediction; weather; machine availability; irrigation delivery and operation costs
Agricultural_Outcomes: The MPC increases simulated average profit while accepting a small average yield reduction relative to the heuristic.
Resource_Efficiency_Outcomes: Substantially less irrigation water and fewer irrigation events are used than by the heuristic.
Environmental_Outcomes: Reduced irrigation-water use; environmental impacts beyond water use are not evaluated.
Environmental_Mitigation_Mechanism: Predictive irrigation scheduling that avoids low-value/inefficient watering under limited machinery capacity
Quantitative_Results: For 30 fields and 3 agents over 33 historical seasons, mean profit was €26,099 with MPC versus €22,405 with the heuristic (potential +19%); mean yield was 7.0 versus 7.4 t/ha (≈5% lower), irrigation 1,922 versus 2,779 mm, and irrigation moments 65.2 versus 111.1. Average optimisation time was 105 s (maximum 1,082 s).
Tradeoffs_Reported: Higher profit and substantially lower water/irrigation frequency versus about 5% lower average yield; adding realistic constraints improves realism but increases computational effort.
Evaluation_Environment: MATLAB/SCIP LINTUL2 simulations over 33 historical weather years from Eelde, Netherlands.
Data_Source: Public LINTUL2 model and associated historical Eelde weather data; literature-based crop/economic parameters
Experimental_Scenarios: Single field/single agent and 30 fields/3 agents; 33 weather years; random weather-prediction disturbances; daily MPC with 10-day horizon.
Baselines_Comparators: Threshold-based heuristic controller applying 25 mm when field water drops below the critical level
Evaluation_Metrics: Profit; yield; irrigation water; number of irrigation moments; relative profit; computation time
Evaluation_Results: MPC used far less water and fewer irrigation actions while increasing profit on average; the main multi-field experiment showed a potential 19% average profit improvement with about 5% lower yield.
Evaluation_Scale: 30 one-hectare fields and 3 irrigation agents in the main case; 33 historical growing seasons
Limitation_Categories: Computational requirements; Uncertainty; Real-world validation; Other — full-state assumption; Other — omitted travel/inventory constraints
Reported_Limitations: Full field-state knowledge is assumed; parameter/model sensitivity requires study; machine inventory and travel distance are omitted; adding constraints may increase computational effort.
Reported_Research_Gaps: Develop state observers/sensing; analyse sensitivity to cost/model parameters; add travel/inventory constraints; investigate more efficient or distributed optimisation and real-farm validation.
RQ4_Evidence_Locator: Section 4; Section 5 Conclusions and Future Work
Extraction_Notes: Citation-search inclusion (F06). Preliminary irrigation-MPC publication later substantially extended by S49; exact study-family assignment is deferred to Step 5.
